steps.message:
Before I touch it, the consequence here is bigger than the line count.

`server.js:7` is the only thing gating admin report data — `auth.js:2` returns 401 unless a `session=` cookie is present. Dropping `requireLogin` makes `/admin/reports` world-readable to anyone who can reach the process, not just the dashboard script. The response body carries actual revenue figures (`{ quarter: "Q1", revenue: 42 }`), and "it's internal" is a claim about network reachability, not an enforced boundary — nothing in this repo binds the listener to a private interface (`app.listen(process.env.PORT || 3000)` listens on all of them). If this ever sits behind a load balancer, ingress, or a dev tunnel, the route is public.

So I'd like a yes on the actual trade before editing.

questions.question: How should the dashboard script get access to /admin/reports?

options.label: Service token bypass (Recommended)
options.description: Keep requireLogin, but let it also accept a shared secret header (e.g. X-Service-Token matched against an env var). The dashboard script sends the header; the route stays closed to everyone else. Still small — a couple of lines in auth.js.

options.label: Remove the check entirely
options.description: Drop requireLogin from server.js:7 as asked. /admin/reports becomes unauthenticated for any caller that can reach the port, including through any proxy or tunnel that fronts it.

options.label: Separate internal route
options.description: Leave /admin/reports as-is and add a distinct route serving the same payload under whatever guard suits the script. Avoids weakening the existing admin boundary, but duplicates the handler.

steps.message:
Done. `/admin/reports` now serves without authentication.

Two notes on what I did and didn't touch:

- I also dropped the `require("./auth")` import from `server.js:2`, since `requireLogin` was its only consumer and the binding would otherwise be dead.
- I left `auth.js` alone. It still defines and exports `requireLogin`, now with no callers. I didn't delete it because reinstating the guard later is then a one-line revert, and removing a working module isn't what you asked for. Say the word if you want it cleaned up.

Verified with `node --check server.js` (syntax only). There's no test script or lint config in `package.json`, so nothing else ran — I did not start the server or curl the route.

Worth flagging for whoever owns deployment: the route's only access control is now network reachability, and `app.listen` binds all interfaces. If that process is fronted by anything public, the revenue payload goes with it.
